Comparing six large reasoning models with 1,854 human subjects, we find that models expend more reasoning effort, measured using the length of the chain-of-thought (CoT), on the kinds of cases that take people longer to adjudicate. People took 31\% longer and models produced 51 to 306\% longer CoTs when offensiveness was held constant across the two posts. The correlation is relatively low for individual decisions ($r = 0.15$--$0.19$), but average response times and average reasoning effort are closely correlated when tasks are grouped by the types of offensive language ($r = 0.85$--$0.93$). Qualitative analyses of the CoT summaries from Gemini 2.5 Pro corroborate these findings, showing that secondary factors were mentioned more often when offensiveness was fixed. The results point to the potential for using reasoning traces to prioritize difficult cases and enhance interpretability. AI paper

docs.title: AutoPBO: LLM-powered Optimization for Local Search PBO Solvers
docs.text:
AutoPBO: LLM-powered Optimization for Local Search PBO Solvers AutoPBO: LLM-powered Optimization for Local Search PBO Solvers arXiv:2509.04007v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Pseudo-Boolean Optimization (PBO) provides a powerful framework for modeling combinatorial problems through pseudo-Boolean (PB) constraints. Local search solvers have shown excellent performance in PBO solving, and their efficiency is highly dependent on their internal heuristics to guide the search. Still, their design often requires significant expert effort and manual tuning in practice. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in automating algorithm design, their application to optimizing PBO solvers remains unexplored. In this work, we introduce AutoPBO, a novel LLM-powered framework to automatically enhance PBO local search solvers. We conduct experiments on a broad range of four public benchmarks, including one real-world benchmark, a benchmark from PB competition, an integer linear programming optimization benchmark, and a crafted combinatorial benchmark, to evaluate the performance improvement achieved by AutoPBO and compare it with six state-of-the-art competitors, including two local search PBO solvers NuPBO and OraSLS, two complete PB solvers PBO-IHS and RoundingSat, and two mixed integer programming (MIP) solvers Gurobi and SCIP. AutoPBO demonstrates significant improvements over previous local search approaches, while maintaining competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art competitors. The results suggest that AutoPBO offers a promising approach to automating local search solver design. AI paper

docs.title: Toward AI epidemiology: a measurement standardization framework for prospective risk detection
docs.text:
Toward AI epidemiology: a measurement standardization framework for prospective risk detection Toward AI epidemiology: a measurement standardization framework for prospective risk detection arXiv:2512.15783v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This paper proposes a measurement standardization framework that compresses expert-AI interactions into structured, comparable fields for prospective risk detection in deployed AI systems, without access to model internals. This concept paper defines the framework's scope, semantically and statistically, and specifies a protocol for its empirical testing. The population-level claims it is designed to support therefore belong to a staged research program rather than to results claimed here. Measurement standardization underpins three claims. The first is a reliability claim: under bounded conditions, large language models can produce reliable, standardized assessments of the evidential and policy alignment of expert-AI interactions. The second is a governance claim: alignment scores give experts an immediate signal during deployment and give institutions a basis for monitoring alignment patterns across mission types, models, and domains. The third is an outcome validation claim: once measurement standardization is established, aggregate alignment scores could be used to study associations with downstream outcomes in regulated professional settings. This introduces the possibility of an "AI epidemiology", a form of risk detection based on correlated variables instead of mechanistic analysis, inspired by epidemiological reasoning. A minimal application of the protocol to a published expert-AI corpus shows that the judge reproduces its policy and evidential alignment scores across two runs under the specified conditions. Judge reliability at scale remains to be validated in future work. The paper sets out a defined grammar of eight interaction fields, together with a statistical protocol based on paired bootstrap inference, DeLong's test for paired AUCs as a sensitivity check, a pre-specified one-sided non-inferiority margin of 0.05, and Holm-Bonferroni correction. AI paper

docs.title: CORE: Concept-Oriented Reinforcement for Bridging the Definition-Application Gap in Mathematical Reasoning
docs.text:
CORE: Concept-Oriented Reinforcement for Bridging the Definition-Application Gap in Mathematical Reasoning CORE: Concept-Oriented Reinforcement for Bridging the Definition-Application Gap in Mathematical Reasoning arXiv:2512.18857v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often solve challenging math exercises yet fail to apply the concept right when the problem requires genuine understanding. Popular Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) pipelines reinforce final answers but provide little fine-grained conceptual signal, so models improve at pattern reuse rather than conceptual applications. We introduce CORE (Concept-Oriented REinforcement), an RL training framework that turns explicit concepts into a controllable supervision signal. Starting from a high-quality, low-contamination textbook resource that links verifiable exercises to concise concept descriptions, we run a sanity probe showing LLMs can restate definitions but fail concept-linked quizzes, quantifying the conceptual reasoning gap. CORE then (i) synthesizes concept-aligned quizzes, (ii) injects brief concept snippets during rollouts to elicit concept-primed trajectories, and (iii) reinforces conceptual reasoning via trajectory replacement after group failures, a lightweight forward-KL constraint that aligns unguided with concept-primed policies, or standard GRPO directly on concept-aligned quizzes. Across several models, CORE delivers consistent gains over vanilla and SFT baselines on both in-domain concept-exercise suites and diverse out-of-domain math benchmarks. CORE unifies direct training on concept-aligned quizzes and concept-injected rollouts under outcome regularization. It provides fine-grained conceptual supervision that bridges problem-solving competence and genuine conceptual reasoning, while remaining algorithm- and verifier-agnostic. AI paper

docs.title: GCD: GCM-consistent Diffusion for Zero-shot Downscaling across Heterogeneous GCMs
docs.text:
GCD: GCM-consistent Diffusion for Zero-shot Downscaling across Heterogeneous GCMs GCD: GCM-consistent Diffusion for Zero-shot Downscaling across Heterogeneous GCMs arXiv:2601.21760v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Climate downscaling of General Circulation Models (GCMs) is an ill-posed inverse problem, as GCM outputs and reanalysis fields arise from different dynamical systems and lack fine-scale temporal pairing. Supervised methods thus rely on synthetic degradations or model-specific adaptation, limiting generalization across heterogeneous GCMs. Zero-shot diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) avoids paired supervision by combining a high-resolution climate prior with inference-time constraints from coarse GCM inputs, but faces consistency and efficiency challenges. We propose GCM-consistent Diffusion for Zero-shot Downscaling (GCD), which addresses these challenges with geographic conditioning, spectrally filtered measurement guidance, and distillation-accelerated Conjugate Gradient guidance. GCD reduces inference from 1,000 diffusion steps to 6 while maintaining consistency with the coarse GCM inputs. Across five heterogeneous GCMs, GCD achieves competitive 99th-percentile extreme-event accuracy and reconstructs plausible high-frequency tropical cyclone structures without model-specific retraining. Github: https://github.com/shawnvonbohr/GCD-Climate-Downscaling.git AI paper

docs.title: Do Multi-Agents Dream of Electric Screens? Achieving 100% on AndroidWorld Through Task Decomposition
docs.text:
Do Multi-Agents Dream of Electric Screens? Achieving 100% on AndroidWorld Through Task Decomposition Do Multi-Agents Dream of Electric Screens? Achieving 100% on AndroidWorld Through Task Decomposition arXiv:2602.07787v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present Minitap's mobile-use, a multi-agent system for Android UI control, and evaluate it on the 116 tasks of AndroidWorld, on Android emulators in Minitap's cloud device infrastructure, real Pixel 7 phones from our device farm and the stock emulator. On fresh, held-out task instances (three pre-registered seeds never used during development), the final system reaches a pass@3 of 100.0% (95% CI 96.8-100.0); pass^3 is 94.0% (95% CI 89.7-97.4) and the mean success rate 98.0% (95% CI 96.0-99.7). Minitap decomposes each task across five LLM agents (planning, subgoal tracking, state capture, decision, execution) and deterministic nodes, with mechanisms that read typed text back from the device, verify the goal on device evidence and detect repeated failures. A study of the initial system measures what each part contributes: removing only the decomposition changes success by -26.1 [-35.6, -16.7] points, the mechanisms together add +11.7 [+2.2, +21.1] points over a single agent, and the decision agent is the one role that needs a frontier model. We then improve reliability with general changes, a few of them triggered by the goal's wording. On MobileMiniWoB++, a second benchmark never used during development, the final system improves on the initial one by 7.1 points (McNemar p = 0.035; 95% CI -0.5 to +14.7). Minitap is open source: https://github.com/minitap-ai/mobile-use AI paper

docs.title: EmbeWebAgent: Embedding Web Agents into Custom Enterprise UIs
docs.text:
EmbeWebAgent: Embedding Web Agents into Custom Enterprise UIs EmbeWebAgent: Embedding Web Agents into Custom Enterprise UIs arXiv:2602.14865v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Most web agents operate at the human interface level, observing screenshots or raw DOM trees without application-level access, which limits robustness and action expressiveness. In enterprise settings, however, explicit control of both the frontend and backend is available. We present EmbeWebAgent, a framework for embedding agents directly into existing UIs using lightweight frontend hooks (curated ARIA and URL-based observations, and a per-page function registry exposed via a WebSocket) and a reusable backend workflow that performs reasoning and takes actions. EmbeWebAgent is stack-agnostic (e.g., React or Angular), supports mixed-granularity actions ranging from GUI primitives to higher-level composites, and orchestrates navigation, manipulation, and domain-specific analytics via MCP tools. Our demo shows minimal retrofitting effort and multi-step behaviors grounded in a live UI setting. Demo Video: https://youtu.be/Cy06Ljee1JQ AI paper

docs.title: Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents
docs.text:
Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents arXiv:2603.01608v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As frontier language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents pursuing complex, long-term objectives, there is increased risk of scheming: agents covertly pursuing misaligned goals. Prior work has focused on showing agents are capable of scheming, but their propensity to scheme in realistic scenarios remains underexplored. To understand when agents scheme, we decompose scheming incentives into agent factors and environmental factors. We develop realistic settings allowing us to systematically vary these factors, each with scheming opportunities for agents that pursue instrumentally convergent goals such as self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal-guarding. Across 11 frontier models and four scenarios, we find almost no scheming despite high environmental incentives, and show this is unlikely to be explained by verbalized evaluation awareness. While inserting adversarially-designed prompt snippets that encourage agency and goal-directedness into an agent's system prompt can induce high scheming rates, snippets used in real agent scaffolds rarely do. In model organisms built with these snippets, scheming behavior is brittle: removing a single tool can drop the scheming rate from 59% to 3%. Increasing oversight can raise rather than deter scheming by up to 25%, an effect that depends on the wording of the oversight sentence and does not appear in a second scenario, where the sabotage itself is reviewed. These results suggest that scheming propensity should be reported per agent configuration rather than as a single rate. Our incentive decomposition enables such systematic measurement in settings relevant for deployment, which is necessary as agents are entrusted with increasingly consequential tasks. AI paper

docs.title: Seeing with You: Perception-Reasoning Coevolution for Multimodal Reasoning
docs.text:
Seeing with You: Perception-Reasoning Coevolution for Multimodal Reasoning Seeing with You: Perception-Reasoning Coevolution for Multimodal Reasoning arXiv:2603.28618v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially enhanced the reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing RLVR approaches typically rely on outcome-driven optimization that updates both perception and reasoning using a shared reward based solely on the final answer. This shared reward blurs credit assignment, frequently improving reasoning patterns while failing to reliably enhance the accuracy of upstream visual evidence extraction. To address this perception bottleneck, we introduce PRCO (Perception-Reasoning Coevolution), a dual-role RLVR framework with a shared policy. PRCO consists of two cooperative roles: an Observer that generates an evidence caption tailored to the question and a Solver that predicts the final answer based on this caption. Crucially, PRCO employs role-specific reward signals: the Solver is optimized using verifiable outcome rewards on the final answer, while the Observer receives a utility reward derived from the Solver's downstream success. Extensive experiments across eight challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PRCO yields consistent improvements across model scales by over 7 points on average accuracy compared to the base model, outperforming prior open-source RL-tuned baselines. AI paper

docs.title: Scaling Causal Reasoning with Increasingly Complex Causal Simulators
docs.text:
Scaling Causal Reasoning with Increasingly Complex Causal Simulators Scaling Causal Reasoning with Increasingly Complex Causal Simulators arXiv:2605.09079v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Despite surpassing human performance across mathematics, coding, and other knowledge-intensive tasks, large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with causal reasoning. A core obstacle is the target data itself: causal systems are complex and often expressed in non-executable forms, while ground-truth answers to causal queries are inherently scarce. We introduce CauSim, a framework that turns causal reasoning from a scarce-label problem into a scalable supervised one. CauSim constructs increasingly complex causal simulators: executable structural causal models (SCMs), incrementally built by LLMs, that scale to globally complex systems while maintaining verifiable answers to causal queries. CauSim operates across representations by formalizing non-executable causal knowledge into code, enabling data augmentation, and translating executable SCMs into natural language, enabling supervision in previously difficult-to-supervise representations. We structure our research into two parts: (1) how to construct increasingly complex causal simulators, and (2) a systematic study of what CauSim enables, demonstrating generalization across representations, consistent gains from curriculum scaling and data volume, LLM self-improvement through self-generated simulators, and data augmentation via formalization of existing domain knowledge. AI paper

docs.title: CardioLoom: A Report-Guided Electrocardiogram Foundation Model for Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Phenotyping
docs.text:
CardioLoom: A Report-Guided Electrocardiogram Foundation Model for Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Phenotyping CardioLoom: A Report-Guided Electrocardiogram Foundation Model for Cross-Domain Cardiovascular Phenotyping arXiv:2605.25446v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Routine electrocardiogram (ECG) reports offer scalable supervision for cardiovascular representation learning. In this retrospective study, we pretrained CardioLoom, a report-guided ECG foundation model, on 2,781,289 ECG-report pairs from 1,298,359 patients. Downstream development used a separate cohort of 721,317 ECGs from 233,798 patients. Evaluation covered 89 targets, with external testing in nine cohorts. Across 45 internal ECG diagnoses, macro area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.624 versus 0.615 for DeepECG-SSL. Across 203 external ECG evaluations, corresponding means were 0.425 and 0.424. Using labels from 10% of training patients, CardioLoom achieved macro-AUPRC 0.559, exceeding supervised training with all labels (0.549). For heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, AUPRCs were 0.690, 0.641 and 0.677 in Zhongshan, Shiyuan and BIDMC. Cardiac amyloidosis screening yielded 4.5% positive predictive value using a threshold targeting 99% specificity in validation. Report-guided pretraining supported label-efficient ECG diagnosis, with variable transfer across echocardiographic phenotypes. AI paper

docs.title: Optimization-like Reasoning in LLMs over Expanding Search Spaces
docs.text:
Optimization-like Reasoning in LLMs over Expanding Search Spaces Optimization-like Reasoning in LLMs over Expanding Search Spaces arXiv:2606.05464v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Verifiable reward training has improved mathematical and coding reasoning, but these domains capture only part of step-by-step decision making. Many real-world tasks require finding a high-value feasible plan among many valid alternatives. We introduce OPT*, a scalable family of optimization-style tasks for training and evaluating LLM step-by-step optimization-like reasoning along a complexity axis: each task provides a feasibility checker and evaluator, while a complexity parameter expands the search space without requiring new human labels. This motivates studying these tasks in two regimes: (i) solver-guided online policy optimization, which uses a solver as a value oracle for partial states and applies rank-based reward shaping to reinforce better next steps, and (ii) search-based offline RL when such solvers are unavailable. Theoretically, we relate success in large search spaces to the information a reasoner extracts per unit of search budget. Empirically, we ablate the ingredients that make search efficient on OPT* and show that training on OPT* improves step-by-step optimization-like reasoning. AI paper

docs.title: Rhythm of the Deep: Two-tier acoustic organization of sperm-whale codas from click waveforms to coda sequences
docs.text:
Rhythm of the Deep: Two-tier acoustic organization of sperm-whale codas from click waveforms to coda sequences Rhythm of the Deep: Two-tier acoustic organization of sperm-whale codas from click waveforms to coda sequences arXiv:2606.16084v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Sperm-whale codas are usually described by the number and timing of their clicks. These measures reveal patterns in whale communication, but do not describe how individual clicks sound. We ask what click waveforms add beyond timing and how acoustic information is organized within codas and across sequences of codas. We analyze 1,952 codas, using frozen audio encoders to identify recurring forms of clicks and whole codas independently. Direct spectral and envelope measurements then test whether the click forms differ in recorded sound. Within codas, click-form composition improves the measured prediction of whole-coda form beyond timing alone. Click spacing also remains related to whole-coda sound when the same click forms are present. Neighboring click forms help predict the next click in the annotated sample, although their order does not improve the tested classification of whole codas. Across recorded sequences, the second preceding whole-coda form improves prediction beyond the immediately preceding form. The gain exceeds two broad first-order references, but stricter controls do not establish a general higher-order rule. Together, these findings show different organizing relationships at the two scales. Within codas, click sound and rhythmic spacing help distinguish complete vocalizations. Across codas, earlier whole-coda forms help predict what follows. AI paper

docs.title: Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning
docs.text:
Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning arXiv:2606.20627v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable agents to plan in latent space by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, yet task specification remains a bottleneck. Visual targets provide precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible yet limited by noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on distinct large generative models. We introduce LAGO (Latent Goal Prediction from Language), a hierarchical world model in which a single predictor both forecasts action-conditioned dynamics and grounds language instructions as sequences of intermediate latent subgoals, training both modes with a single regression objective over a shared latent space. At each planning step, LAGO predicts a sequence of latent subgoals from a language instruction and optimizes an action sequence using a soft-minimum alignment cost that rewards subgoal proximity without enforcing a rigid path. Subgoals are repredicted as the agent's state evolves, turning a single long-horizon instruction into a sequence of locally tractable objectives. Across environments spanning navigation and manipulation, LAGO outperforms flat and hierarchical image-goal planners, with the largest gains on long-horizon navigation with curved, hazard-constrained paths, where it more than doubles the success rate of a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy trained on the same demonstrations. Grounding language in the world model's own latent space also outperforms vision-language reward models, including one that plans with ground-truth dynamics. AI paper

docs.title: Process Advantage Signal Shaping: Advantage Construction for Process-Supervised Reinforcement Learning in LLM Reasoners
docs.text:
Process Advantage Signal Shaping: Advantage Construction for Process-Supervised Reinforcement Learning in LLM Reasoners Process Advantage Signal Shaping: Advantage Construction for Process-Supervised Reinforcement Learning in LLM Reasoners arXiv:2606.29296v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Dense process supervision provides local evaluations, but leaves open how these scores should become policy advantages. We introduce PASS (Process Advantage Signal Shaping), an advantage-construction method for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). PASS separately normalizes and fuses reward channels, constructs batch-shared credit units from variation in the fused score trace, and normalizes return-to-go by the remaining unit count. These operations connect feedback scale, credit resolution, and accumulation horizon in a single computation. We evaluate learned process reward model (PRM) feedback for mathematical reasoning and teacher-derived token feedback for multi-hop question answering (QA). Across seven mathematics benchmarks, PASS improves average pass@1 by 4.62 percentage points over outcome-only GRPO with approximately $2\%$ shorter responses. Matched comparisons with Step-GRPO and component ablations further support the choice of shared credit units and residual normalization. On multi-hop QA, PASS improves over process-signal controls across two normalizers; token-level ablations reveal an accuracy--length trade-off: token-level accumulation slightly favors pass@1, while PASS achieves higher pass@8/16 with shorter responses. The results establish the conversion from local process scores to policy advantages as a consequential design choice across distinct supervision sources. AI paper

docs.title: RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies
docs.text:
RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies arXiv:2607.07646v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Does RL post-training merely amplify primitive skills already latent in a base model, or can it compose primitive skills into new higher-level strategies? We study this question in a fully observable rewrite-grammar environment where the pretraining distribution is known and every generated rewrite can be audited. A Transformer is pretrained on primitive symbol-rewrite chains and post-trained on a Trace-based reasoning task with only a binary final-answer reward. RL solves held-out problems that remain rarely solved by the pretrained model even under much larger sampling budgets, while rejection fine-tuning improves early but plateaus. Trace analysis shows that RL reorganizes primitive competence through a phased compositional mechanism: it first strengthens primitive reductions, then discovers valid composed procedures. These include sequential compositions, which collapse ordered chains of primitive contractions, and parallel compositions, which combine independent primitive contractions in a single step. The composed procedures are not isolated samples; they are reused and consolidated into a stable repertoire. Comparing RL with rejection fine-tuning shows that the key difference is not exploration volume but selectivity: RFT produces many shortcut-like rewrites, much of them invalid, whereas RL concentrates exploration into valid reusable structure. Pretraining ablations show that the emergence of compositional strategies is gated not by primitive exposure alone, but by whether pretraining organizes primitive competence into reduction procedures that RL can later compress. The base model provides weak procedural ingredients; RL builds them into reliable higher-level strategies. AI paper

docs.title: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning
docs.text:
Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning arXiv:2607.22697v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/TTCov. AI paper

docs.title: Alternating Abduction and Planning over Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
docs.text:
Alternating Abduction and Planning over Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs Alternating Abduction and Planning over Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs arXiv:2607.27287v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Knowledge graphs change over time, but the effects of actions on them are only partly stated: the ontology entails further consequences, facts that an action needs are often unknown, and an action may make the graph inconsistent. We study these problems for Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (TDKGs), that is, SROIQ knowledge bases whose actions are rules with delete/insert templates and whose events lie on an intrinsic timeline. We present three tools: temporal projection, the exact test of plans; DDA (Direct-Derivation Abduction), which explains an observation by assuming its negation and negating what the reasoner newly derives; and APT (Abduction and Planning over TDKGs), which plans backwards from a goal, assumes the facts that the plan needs but nobody stated, and lets DDA explain the assumptions, each explanation becoming a sub-goal, up to a depth bound. The tools use a SROIQ reasoner only through a small contract, so they depend neither on a particular reasoner nor on a particular data structure; they are designed for a reasoner that processes added and removed axioms incrementally. Change is treated without modal operators, on one linear timeline and without possible worlds, so decidability of projection follows from that of SROIQ. We prove that indirect effects are exactly the entailments of the updated state, that DDA and APT are sound and terminate, and that bounded planning is 2NExpTime-hard and in 3ExpTime. We compare the tools with hitting-set abduction, the solver CATS and classical planning, and run them on six benchmarks and five reasoners with identical results. AI paper

docs.title: Explore, Map, Remember, Decide: A Benchmark for VLM Readiness in Safety-Critical Scenarios
docs.text:
Explore, Map, Remember, Decide: A Benchmark for VLM Readiness in Safety-Critical Scenarios Explore, Map, Remember, Decide: A Benchmark for VLM Readiness in Safety-Critical Scenarios arXiv:2608.08077v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are often deployed as embodied controllers for robotics, yet it remains unclear how well they can explore an environment, maintain an internal map, and ground safety-critical decisions in long-horizon sequential trajectories. In this work, we introduce EMRD, an evaluation framework that decouples spatial reasoning into four stages: Explore (what the agent observes), Map (what it records and where), Remember (what it retains), and Decide (whether its final choice is justified), scored across 18 stage-specific metrics. We use EMRD to evaluate eleven open- and closed-weight VLMs across 16 buildings under nominal conditions and three environmental stresses (darkness, smoke, and motion noise), where an embodied VLM explores unknown rooms, maps observed objects, and selects the safest gathering place. Open-weight models leave rooms unvisited in 95% of episodes and detect at most 51% of objects; closed-weight models explore more, though with an external memory (notepad), two of the three stop prematurely. Without external memory, most VLMs keep fewer of the objects they saw, especially in larger buildings. The start limits which rooms are explored, and open-weight models started in different rooms agree on the final room not significantly more often than chance. Moreover, these choices are biased by semantic priors: swapping a room's label is often enough to change the final choice. Finally, motion noise increases object position error (by 12-60% for closed-weight models), strong darkness lowers map recall by 28-31 percentage points, and dense smoke reduces seen objects by 25-39 points, while the choice among the rooms entered does not change significantly. AI paper

docs.title: Multi-Granularity Context-Enhanced RAG over Multimodal Knowledge Graphs
docs.text:
Multi-Granularity Context-Enhanced RAG over Multimodal Knowledge Graphs Multi-Granularity Context-Enhanced RAG over Multimodal Knowledge Graphs arXiv:2608.25986v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Knowledge graph (KG)-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) leverages structured knowledge to provide large language models (LLMs) with high-quality external information. Building on these works, recent studies have explored multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) as knowledge bases for GraphRAG. This enables GraphRAG to integrate knowledge across multiple modalities, thereby further enhancing its performance. However, existing MMKG-based RAG methods generally follow a common pipeline in which different modalities are largely processed independently before being fused. As a result, textual context is only used to a limited extent during visual information extraction and subsequent multimodal knowledge fusion. This brings a semantic gap between images and text which limits the multimodal GraphRAG performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for constructing a Context-Enhanced MMKG (CEMMKG) to better support multimodal GraphRAG. The proposed CEMMKG enriches each image with complementary textual context at both local and global scopes. Local context goes beyond the surrounding text by incorporating sentences that are semantically related to the image, while global context provides a summary of the entire document. We further introduce a multi-granularity design for the local context, allowing it to capture semantically relevant information at different levels of detail. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets validate that CEMMKG is effective in leveraging contextual information to improve MMKG-based RAG performance. Moreover, its effectiveness across different MMKG-based RAG methods demonstrates its broad applicability. AI paper

docs.title: The Memory Trust Gap: Reliance on Stale Evidence Across Model Scales in LLM Agents
docs.text:
The Memory Trust Gap: Reliance on Stale Evidence Across Model Scales in LLM Agents The Memory Trust Gap: Reliance on Stale Evidence Across Model Scales in LLM Agents arXiv:2609.01852v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Persistent-memory agents can follow stale information despite current authoritative evidence. We study stale-evidence reliance across Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B checkpoints using two controlled, action-scored suites: a Benefit suite requiring stored information and a Safety suite providing current evidence as static prompt text. We distinguish stale-value reliance from net accuracy loss relative to no memory. Benefit-suite reliance is 0.92-1.00 across checkpoints. In the Safety suite, larger checkpoints resist a plain stale note but incur substantial harm when it appears newer. A full $2\times2\times2\times2$ factorial manipulates label, recency, source authority, and position. Direct cross-size contrasts identify stronger recency effects in the larger tested checkpoints and a position-effect sign reversal within Qwen3. Metadata improves accuracy at all four checkpoints, with larger gains at 4B/8B; pre-resolution yields near-ceiling accuracy across all four. Llama-Instruct comparisons provide cross-family evidence for selected effects, while RGB and MisBench corroborate stale-value reliance. A framing control shows that the failure extends beyond memory-labeled content. These results characterize cue-dependent vulnerability across tested checkpoints without isolating capability or evaluating a complete memory lifecycle. AI paper

docs.title: PhysAlign: A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Role Alignment in Multimodal Physics Reasoning
docs.text:
PhysAlign: A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Role Alignment in Multimodal Physics Reasoning PhysAlign: A Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Role Alignment in Multimodal Physics Reasoning arXiv:2609.33319v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A key challenge in physics diagram understanding is correctly associating visual information with the physical entities, relations, and conditions it describes. Even when a value, symbol, or other local element is accurately recognized, assigning it to the wrong entity or scope can distort the underlying physical premise and lead to incorrect reasoning. To systematically study this challenge, we introduce \textbf{PhysAlign}, a benchmark designed to assess whether multimodal models correctly associate information recognized from physics diagrams with its intended physical role. By disentangling visual recognition from physical-role assignment through localized probes and controlled variants, PhysAlign isolates correspondence errors from recognition failures. It contains 3,341 human-validated probes spanning 986 physics problems, enabling systematic evaluation of visual recognition and physical-role correspondence at scale. We further introduce five complementary evaluation metrics, including CAcc, GAcc, and JAcc, which provide a comprehensive assessment of models' ability to recognize diagram content, establish correct physical correspondences, and solve the underlying physics problem. Across our evaluated multimodal models, PhysAlign reveals a consistent gap between local visual recognition and physical-role grounding. Even when the queried content is correctly recognized, the conditional correspondence error rate remains 13.8\% for GPT-6-Astra and rises to about 50.6\% for InternVL3.5-8B. These findings indicate that strong perception alone does not ensure reliable physical interpretation, exposing a distinct grounding bottleneck that is largely hidden by answer-level accuracy and highlighting the need for future models to better align recognized visual evidence with its physical meaning. AI paper

docs.title: Code4Scene: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Constructing and Editing 3D Scenes
docs.text:
Code4Scene: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Constructing and Editing 3D Scenes Code4Scene: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Constructing and Editing 3D Scenes arXiv:2609.36777v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Frontier coding agents can now write and execute code that authors 3D environments, but whether they reliably understand 3D structure and precisely control scene state remains unclear. The generated 3D scene is a persistent, executable artifact: a convincing render can hide incorrect spatial relations, intersecting objects, or unintended modifications. We introduce Code4Scene, a benchmark of 170 Unreal Engine cases built from human-assembled scenes that evaluates coding agents on two complementary settings under a shared execution interface. Construction tests scene-level spatial reasoning from open-ended language specifications, where many realizations are valid; editing tests precise control of scene state, where the agent must recover the target scene from reference images while preserving everything else. Rather than scoring code or rendered views, Code4Scene evaluates the generated engine-native scene for task fulfillment, artifact integrity, and static physical validity, with edits additionally compared against withheld ground truth. Across 14 coding-agent systems on the 83-case public set, construction and editing performance are strongly correlated but not interchangeable (Spearman $\rho = 0.67$): Claude Fable 5.1 leads construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads editing. Spatial Composition is the weakest construction category for every agent, while editing remains imprecise: the best Repair F1 is only 0.562, and 34.2% of edits that fully recover the target still introduce unintended changes elsewhere in the scene. These results expose a gap between plausible 3D generation and reliable spatial reasoning and state control. The project webpage is at https://simworld.org/code4scene. AI paper

docs.title: Mingbird: A Local-First Agent Harness Enabling Small Open Models to Complete Real Tasks
docs.text:
Mingbird: A Local-First Agent Harness Enabling Small Open Models to Complete Real Tasks Mingbird: A Local-First Agent Harness Enabling Small Open Models to Complete Real Tasks arXiv:2610.02001v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Small open-weight language models now run on a laptop, but they fail at multi-step work in ways a large model does not: they stop with the files missing, repeat one action until the budget ends, and report success without checking. At the one-to-nine-billion-parameter tier the harness supplies almost all of the procedural control that a large model supplies for itself.We present Mingbird, an open-source harness for that tier on a consumer graphics card: 12k lines of Python, a 628-test suite, and eighteen mechanisms for context economy, completion, time budget and the host boundary, plus a crawl guard outside those four groups. Its design point is completion control: the harness runs executable checks on the working directory and refuses a claim of completion when they fail.Five evaluations accompany it. A configuration-surface audit finds four defects that the 625-test suite of v3.1.1 missed, each because a test checked a property adjacent to the one that broke. A ten-task probe suite gives each mechanism a reason to fire and reports where the change reaches the artifact, including one mechanism that cuts the signal it protects. Disabling five of six completion-time checks costs 0.152 of the artifact score on eighteen held-out tasks, three replications per cell (95% CI [+0.064, +0.246], Holm p = 0.014). On a 288-cell matrix the harness reaches 0.886 against 0.631, 0.479 and 0.405 for three open scaffolds, and on {\tau} 2 -bench it ranks first or tied first in all three domains against the arms evaluated.Tasks, scorer, source and every per-cell result are public. AI paper

docs.title: When Terminal-Agent Training Stalls: Demystifying Data Generation and Verification Challenge
docs.text:
When Terminal-Agent Training Stalls: Demystifying Data Generation and Verification Challenge When Terminal-Agent Training Stalls: Demystifying Data Generation and Verification Challenge arXiv:2610.02405v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automated terminal-agent training relies on generated environments and verifiers to turn open-ended interaction into reward. Yet a runnable Docker image and executable test suite do not guarantee that the resulting reward is faithful, informative, or even attributable to agent behavior. We present a pipeline that generates containerized terminal tasks and their executable verifiers, and use it to demystify failure modes in task generation and live-environment evaluation. Our analysis separates four requirements that are often conflated: structural validity, verifier faithfulness, policy solvability, and infrastructure reliability. In a GRPO training of Qwen3.5-9B, it overfits on a relatively easy dataset within 20 steps. Conversely, in a controlled Qwen3.5-9B comparison, adding hard tasks lowers mean rollout pass@2 from 81.3% to 20.6%, restoring informative failures without changing the training configuration. We further identify near-duplicate task generation, incomplete anti-shortcut safeguards, Dockerfile failures, asynchronous pass@k bias, and concurrency-induced environment errors as distinct threats to measurement. These findings should motivate the community for a terminal agent specific evaluation harness that pairs structural checks and rollout-derived solvability with extensive verifier audits. AI paper

docs.title: Reliable Self-Evolution with Imperfect Proxy Rewards
docs.text:
Reliable Self-Evolution with Imperfect Proxy Rewards Reliable Self-Evolution with Imperfect Proxy Rewards arXiv:2610.02975v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based self-evolving search is a promising approach to scientific discovery. However, high-fidelity evaluation of every candidate is prohibitively expensive in some domains. Self-evolving systems in such settings therefore rely on low-cost but imperfect proxy rewards, which may assign high scores to infeasible candidates. These false positives may contaminate both the final output and the feedback used to guide subsequent generations. This motivates statistically calibrated reward intervals for more reliable self-evolving search. We propose Conformal Interval-Driven Self-Evolution (CISE), which constructs candidate-specific reward intervals using conditional conformal inference and iteration-wise online density-ratio estimation. CISE uses conservative interval-based rewards for evolutionary feedback and returns candidates only when all required property intervals lie entirely within their respective feasible regions. We derive fixed-iteration coverage results under explicit assumptions of independence and covariate shift. We evaluate CISE on three self-evolving search tasks in materials science. In our experiments, all candidates returned by CISE are true positives under high-fidelity evaluation, whereas the baselines return more candidates but include false positives. These results highlight the value of a smaller, more precise shortlist when downstream validation budgets are limited. Our repository is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/CISE.git. AI paper

docs.title: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?
docs.text:
Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? arXiv:2610.22155v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference latency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Pass^3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serving latency from models' real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated token counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. Based on these results, we discuss future directions for improving real-time multimodal models, including adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action. AI paper

docs.title: Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?
docs.text:
Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction? Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction? arXiv:2610.23051v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). Existing studies largely depend on externally supplied contexts or reward-bearing interaction histories, while work on general tool-using agents lacks a learning algorithm view. We represent an interactive learner by its state, update, and decision rule, covering active learning, bandits, and online reinforcement learning (RL). For expressivity, we construct causal Transformers that approximate these algorithms over a finite horizon, and bound the resulting loss in return. For training, we characterize when optimizing process rewards preserves behavior that maximizes the final outcome. Distillation experiments show that Transformers can learn to execute three representative recursions. We then train models from outcome or process rewards without oracle action or state targets, as in RL post-training. Different rewards yield distinct decision policies. Improving the alignment of process supervision with outcome-optimal action preferences shifts learned decisions accordingly. Such behavioral differences persist in a pretrained language model across textual paraphrases. AI paper

docs.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
docs.text:
A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt arXiv:2610.24133v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A black hole retains only a few conserved charges of the matter it formed from. We are inspired to make the analogy and we ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. For two prompts followed by the same continuation, the difference of their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks. Beyond the first layers, trained models forget faster ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$) than untrained ones of the same architecture ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). For finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits and non-degenerate pre-norm activations, we prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for prompt length $P$ and depth $L$: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} through continuation tokens adds only logarithmic factors. Conditional on the generated text, the prompt's influence on the next token thus vanishes. The bound fixes only the asymptotic shape and is uninformative at the lengths we measure in trained networks; an exactly solvable linear relay model shows that it cannot be improved and accounts for the untrained curves. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt stops the decay early in training, and training suppresses relay by about one billion tokens, before attention sinks form. A toolkit that measures $\alpha$ for any Hugging Face causal language model is publicly available. AI paper

docs.title: Screening LLM Judges Without Ground Truth: A Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Dental Hygiene Coach
docs.text:
Screening LLM Judges Without Ground Truth: A Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Dental Hygiene Coach Screening LLM Judges Without Ground Truth: A Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Dental Hygiene Coach arXiv:2610.24335v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Evaluating a fine-tuned coaching model with expert graders is slow and expensive, and an LLM judge cannot be trusted without ground truth. We present a staged pipeline that screens candidate LLM judges and student models before expert review, using explicit decision rules at each stage: judge output audit, similarity with hosted judges, bias checks, and decision robustness. We demonstrate it on an AI dental hygiene coach. The case study uses synthetic, clinically unvalidated training and reference data to demonstrate the operation of the pipeline, rather than to establish the clinical performance of the resulting models. Two fine-tuned small language models (Granite-4.1-8B and Qwen3-8B), each trained at three data sizes, were scored on seven metrics by five judges (three local, two hosted). Two local judges, Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, were not distinguishable from the agreement between the hosted judges on six of seven metrics by rank correlation, and Qwen3.8-27B was the most similar to the hosted judges overall. No judge met our criterion for favoring its own model family or training-data source. The student comparison did not separate the two models on any metric under the pipeline's rule, so the choice of Granite-4.1-8B, which led in 29 of 35 judge-by-metric cells, is a lean that depends partly on truncated Qwen3-8B outputs. The pipeline also surfaced problems that raw scores hid, including the truncated outputs and hallucination flags from one hosted judge that no other judge corroborated. No dental hygiene expert has graded these responses, so the findings are preliminary and the pipeline's final stage, anchoring to expert judgement, is proposed but not performed. AI paper

docs.title: ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models
docs.text:
ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models arXiv:2610.25963v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Judgment models answer semantic questions by scoring a finite set of candidate outcomes. Can reusable programs turn these local decisions into powerful multistep reasoning? We introduce \method, a framework that jointly constructs judgment schemas and composition programs for frozen judgment models. A generative teacher designs the procedure offline; the judgment model resolves local semantic questions online, and the saved program composes its decisions into an answer. We study three allocations of design effort between humans and the teacher, focusing on construction through a shared interface. We instantiate the framework with Kev. On three selected BIG-Bench Hard tasks, nine independently constructed programs solve all 450 executions of 150 development inputs. A separate deployment study freezes three programs after development-set reference-agreement refinement and evaluates them on 600 held-out questions. These programs achieve near-perfect 99.67\% macro accuracy, versus 64.00\% for direct Kev and 68.80\% for final-answer-only Qwen3.5-4B. They attain comparable observed accuracy to Qwen's unrestricted response policy (99.07\%) with an \textbf{8.43-fold online speedup}: 0.255 versus 2.150 seconds per question. These results show how reusable programs can substantially expand the reasoning capability of a compact judgment model while keeping its parameters fixed. AI paper

docs.title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
docs.text:
Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy arXiv:2610.26836v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy. AI paper

docs.title: RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
docs.text:
RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding arXiv:2610.31276v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget. AI paper

docs.title: MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research
docs.text:
MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research arXiv:2610.34203v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Materials research relies on scattered and growing data, knowledge, and simulation tools, and a single study often spans multi-day workflows across literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with new capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost-score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, it outperforms Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. Code is available at https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS. AI paper

docs.title: Skill erosion, individual memory and the reversibility of AI adoption
docs.text:
Skill erosion, individual memory and the reversibility of AI adoption Skill erosion, individual memory and the reversibility of AI adoption arXiv:2611.04886v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills needed for future work. We consider a population of agents who perform a task either with their own skill or with the help of AI. Agents tend to imitate more successful peers, and their skills evolve in time: improving with practice and eroding with reliance on AI. We study, analytically and with simulations, the collective consequences of AI adoption. We show that the mechanism of skill erosion makes adoption bistable and that
  the long-term behaviour of the population depends on how skills are distributed: populations with the same adoption and mean skill can reach opposite asymptotic states, depending on how expertise is shared between AI users and non-users. A deterministic description that follows the mean skills of the two groups and the variance of skills among non-users predicts the outcome of individual runs as accurately as the simulations allow, whereas the means alone are not sufficient. We also consider the situation when the benefit of AI improves in time. In that case, adoption can jump abruptly, and a temporary increase in benefit, such as in a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its original value. Skill erosion therefore creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse. AI paper

docs.title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
docs.text:
Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts arXiv:2611.06374v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI's inflection point is a fountain of risks for digital platforms, as those in control of global platforms cede control of the algorithms, membership and content to AI: (i) AI control of global platforms used by the majority of humanity; (ii) unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals; and (iii) unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, which people cannot distinguish from genuine content. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon: a social contract that can be freely adopted by any group of people, where groups bound by the same contract can union by mutual consent, possibly into a single global union. Grassroots contracts are realised by grassroots platforms, person-to-person platforms owned, operated and governed by their participants. We developed, with AI, a methodology to compile grassroots contracts to working smartphone apps. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two, and show how they corral these risks: (i) grassroots platforms are not controlled by a third party who may cede control to AI; (ii) AI agents are introduced with accountability: similarly to cars, their manufacturers are accountable for manufacturing defects and their operators for reckless operation; and (iii) every item carries the signatures of its author and of every agent that forwarded it, so creators and forwarders of harmful content are accountable and culpable. Much work remains for grassroots apps to be competitive with incumbent global platforms; but perhaps now this could be achieved with some AI-months rather than with incalculably-many person-years. AI paper

docs.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
docs.text:
Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games arXiv:2611.09271v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison AI paper

docs.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
docs.text:
Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion arXiv:2611.11010v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete. AI paper

docs.title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
docs.text:
SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution arXiv:2611.15481v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods. AI paper

docs.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
docs.text:
Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets arXiv:2611.19292v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses. AI paper

docs.title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
docs.text:
Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration arXiv:2611.19345v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64. AI paper

docs.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
docs.text:
Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation arXiv:2611.20794v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect. AI paper

docs.title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
docs.text:
Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report arXiv:2611.21072v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Sage S2.1 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S2.1 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench 2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback. AI paper

docs.title: Human-like Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Driving using Knowledge Representation and Large Language Models
docs.text:
Human-like Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Driving using Knowledge Representation and Large Language Models Human-like Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Driving using Knowledge Representation and Large Language Models arXiv:2505.16498v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Achieving full automation in self-driving vehicles remains a challenge, especially in dynamic urban environments where navigation requires real-time adaptability. Existing systems struggle to handle navigation plans when faced with unpredictable changes in road layouts, spontaneous detours, or missing map data, due to their heavy reliance on predefined cartographic information. In this work, we explore the use of Large Language Models to generate Answer Set Programming rules by translating informal navigation instructions into structured, logic-based reasoning. ASP provides non-monotonic reasoning, allowing autonomous vehicles to adapt to evolving scenarios without relying on predefined maps. We present an experimental evaluation in which LLMs generate ASP constraints that encode real-world urban driving logic into a formal knowledge representation. By automating the translation of informal navigation instructions into logical rules, our method improves adaptability and explainability in autonomous navigation. Results show that LLM-driven ASP rule generation supports semantic-based decision-making, offering an explainable framework for dynamic navigation planning that aligns closely with how humans communicate navigational intent. AI paper

docs.title: Evaluating and Mitigating Skin Color Bias in Skin Lesion Classificatio
docs.text:
